_comment: USER-FACING highlights for the release named by `version`, published to the website as
part of https://devicechain.io/releases.json (see hack/build-release-manifest.sh).
🔴 UPDATE THIS IN THE PR THAT PREPARES A RELEASE, BEFORE TAGGING — and update `version`,
`theme`, `breaking` and `highlights` TOGETHER. They are one record of one release, and
the way this file goes wrong is three of the four moving while the fourth keeps last
release's answer: a theme naming work that is not in the highlights below it reads as
confidently as one that is. The `guard` job fails
the release when `version` does not match the tag, deliberately and as the FIRST job —
so a forgotten update costs nothing but a re-run, rather than publishing last release's
highlights against this release's version. Confidently wrong is worse than absent, and
this file is the one part of the manifest a machine cannot derive.
`theme` IS THE ONE PHRASE THAT NAMES THE RELEASE — a chapter title, not a changelog
line. It leads the GitHub release notes and it reaches releases.json, so it is the
first thing a reader decides against. A good one names what changed about the system:
"the instance is declared, not remembered". A bad one is a category ("bug fixes and
improvements"), the version restated, or the first highlight with its verbs filed off —
if it would fit any release, it is not this release's theme.
Write a PHRASE. The guard caps it at 72 characters, the width of a commit subject,
because past that you are writing a sentence, and a sentence about what changed is a
highlight — there is already a list for those below. The cap is the only taste this
file can enforce; the rest is on you.
🔴 The theme is PUBLISHED, and so is every highlight — into the GitHub release body and
into devicechain.io/releases.json. No ADR references in either: ADRs live in a repo the
reader cannot open, so a citation is a dead reference dressed as a source. Say the thing
itself, or link to a public page. THIS BLOCK IS DIFFERENT — `_comment` is published
nowhere, it is the only part of the file a reader never sees, and it may cite ADR-080 or
any other freely. The guard reads exactly that distinction: it scans `theme` and
`highlights[]`, case-insensitively, and leaves this block alone.
WRITE FOR SOMEONE DECIDING WHETHER TO UPGRADE, not for someone reading the commit log.
The changelog is already generated from commit subjects and is right there in the release
notes; repeating `fix(events): give payload rows and anchors identities of their own` here
adds nothing. Say what changed for the person running the platform.
Keep it to a handful of lines. This renders in the website's download menu, not in a
document — a fifteen-item list is a changelog wearing a different hat.
`breaking` MEANS 'THIS RELEASE HAS BREAKING CHANGES'. It does NOT mean 'you must recreate
your instance', and this comment used to say it did — it told you to set the flag when an
upgrade is not a plain `helm upgrade`. The website has not read it that way since the
copy was repaired: `true` renders exactly one sentence, 'This release has breaking changes
— read the release notes before upgrading', and `false` renders nothing at all. So set it
true whenever something breaks for SOMEBODY — an API caller, an operator, a package
consumer — and use the first highlight to say who, and whether the upgrade itself is
ordinary. If a release ever genuinely requires recreating an instance, give that its OWN
manifest field rather than overloading this one a second time.
The other correction: there is no docs banner. Nothing under docs/ fetches releases.json.
The website download menu is this file's only consumer.
For each highlight, ask whether it makes a sentence on the marketing site stale. The
site is a separate repository and nothing here reads its prose. Answering "no site
impact" is a fine answer; not asking is not.
theme: sign in through your own identity provider; widgets ship as packages
highlights: This release breaks things for operators, API callers and package consumers, so read the upgrade guide first; the upgrade from v0.19.0 is in place (`dcctl install`, then `dcctl upgrade`). Before you upgrade: rename `ingestRateLimit.messagesPerSecond` to `ingestRateLimit.readingsPerSecond` and `outboundMessagesPerSecond` to `outboundCallsPerSecond` in any service settings you set, or those services refuse to start; move every device that uses an X.509 credential to an access token or an MQTT password, because X.509 credentials are no longer accepted; and give an S3 object store's credential `s3:ListBucket`. On its first start `event-management` builds two event-store indexes, and above 4,000,000 uncompressed rows or 500 chunks it refuses until you build them by hand as the guide shows. While `event-sources` and `device-management` run different versions, events that carry a device password or access token in their body can be refused, so upgrade them together. After the upgrade everyone signs in again once, and each dashboard published before it must be published again before viewers see it. An account whose stored email address is not in its canonical form can no longer sign in until an administrator recreates it. Device passwords are converted to a one-way digest, so going back to v0.19.0 afterwards leaves devices that use an MQTT password unable to authenticate. API callers: the tenant ceiling fields are now `ingestReadingsPerSecond` and `outboundCallsPerSecond`, `publishDashboard` and the `dashboards` search return new types, reading a dashboard's draft needs `dashboard:write`, `bucketedMeasurements` needs a `startTime`, a new MQTT password must be at least 16 bytes, and lookups of more than 1,000 keys and many oversized inputs are refused with `LIMIT_EXCEEDED`. Package consumers: `@devicechain/widgets` no longer exports `WIDGET_REGISTRY`, `ALARM_WIDGET_REGISTRY`, `CONTROL_WIDGET_REGISTRY`, `SELECTION_WIDGET_REGISTRY` or `LOCATION_WIDGET_REGISTRY`, needs the new `@devicechain/widget-sdk` installed beside it, and no longer brings `echarts`, which your app now declares itself; dashboard bindings move from `DashboardHubConfig` to `DashboardRenderer`.

People can sign in through your own OpenID Connect identity provider. A superuser connects a provider for the instance or for chosen tenants, and the console, the dashboard app and the MCP authorization page then offer single sign-on. Accounts can be created at first sign-in, provider groups can map to tenant roles, and a tenant can require single sign-on. Nothing changes until a connection exists, and password sign-in keeps working. Signing out now ends the session on the server, a sign-in lasts at most 7 days, and on an instance served over HTTPS the chart now derives the public address that sign-in needs, which also turns on the OAuth authorization server that MCP clients use.

Dashboards can show widgets from your own packages. The new `@devicechain/widget-sdk` package defines a widget, its settings and its editor; the eleven built-in widgets register through the same interface, and the console and the dashboard app share one registry that includes the packages you add when you build them. A dashboard keeps a widget it cannot resolve exactly as stored and shows a placeholder, and the console will not publish a version until it resolves. Publishing now makes a version live for viewers, an earlier version can be made live again, and a dashboard's draft is visible only to its authors.

Devices can receive configuration. A device profile declares which shared attributes its devices may see; each change becomes a numbered revision sent to the device over MQTT, the device reports whether it applied it, and the console shows both. Over-the-air updates arrive as a first slice in the opt-in `update-management` service: an artifact catalogue with a verified upload, assignment to single devices, a resumable download, and every attempt tracked. No artifact can be assigned until you allow unverified artifacts, because nothing yet authenticates who produced one, and there are no fleet rollouts yet. `dcctl bootstrap --object-store` gives a new instance the object store that artifacts and tenant logos need; an existing instance does not gain one on upgrade. An MQTT device password is now stored only as a keyed digest and shown once, and device passwords and access tokens no longer cross the event stream as sent.

The services that handle every event do less work for it. They now run Go's garbage collector at `GOGC=400` with a soft memory limit, which on Google Kubernetes Engine at 6,000 events a second cut CPU per event by 18% in `device-management` and `event-management`, 15% in `device-state` and 4 to 5% in the other two. `device-management` keeps its lookups for 5 minutes rather than 5 seconds, so devices that report less often than every 5 seconds are now answered from memory, and every change evicts them on every replica. Size each replica's caches for the whole active fleet, and note that a replica that misses an eviction can accept a revoked device credential's events for up to those 5 minutes. Readers fetch their next batch ahead by default, which keeps the detection engine's backlog small under heavy load without raising throughput. Live detection now reads back events it was not delivered instead of skipping them, and every binary is built with Go 1.26.9.

The documentation is now also in Simplified Chinese, and adds a reference page for each GraphQL schema, the device protocol as JSON Schemas, every `dcctl` command and the services' metrics, and a runbook entry for every shipped alert.
